body:
Although the project's website says it is an "OpenSSL exception", the text is quite different than the existing OpenSSL exceptions, and the SPDX diff tool shows no close matches. I agree with adding it. 
Do we want to include GPL in the license identifier as we have for other exceptions?

~Note that there is likely a typo in the exception text (the "special exception" paragraph mentions LGPL in the first sentence and GPL in the second sentence).~ Sorry, I wasn't reading carefully enough, I believe @swinslow is correct in his subsequent comment!

+1 to add as a new exception with `stunnel-exception` as the ID and "stunnel Exception" as the name. More details below:

= = = = =

This exception is somewhat similar to [GPL-3.0-interface-exception](https://spdx.org/licenses/GPL-3.0-interface-exception.html), but has enough differences that I don't think it would be appropriate to accommodate it within that identifier via further markup.

As just one example, this stunnel version doesn't include the requirement at the end of the third paragraph of GPL-3.0-interface-exception that if you modify the _interface_, then the exception does not apply to modified versions and must be removed.

Interestingly (to me anyway), the stunnel exception appears to be derived from the GPL-3.0 sample exception language, but stunnel is using it with GPL-2.0(-or-later).

@richardfontana I don't think that's actually a typo... I think this originates from a modified version of https://www.gnu.org/licenses/gpl-faq.en.html#LinkingOverControlledInterface (which is what was used for GPL-3.0-interface-exception). From a brief read I'm not clear on the intent behind referencing LGPL specifically there, but either way, it's present also in the version that originated from the FSF and is on the License List.

I think this pretty clearly fits into the [Exception Inclusion Principles](https://github.com/spdx/license-list-XML/blob/main/DOCS/license-inclusion-principles.md#license-exceptions):

* it is not a stand-alone license
* it grants an additional permission and/or an exception to a license condition
* it doesn't impose additional restrictions
* it has actual, substantial use based on being used in Fedora

Given that, I'm +1 to add as noted above.
